steps.body: Legend says young Gauss was told to add 1 through 100 as busywork — and answered in seconds. His move: **pair the ends inward**. 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98, … every pair adds to the same 101, and 100 numbers make 50 pairs: 50 × 101 = 5050. A staircase of terms, folded flat.

widget.prompt: Pairing 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 100 from the ends inward, what does EACH pair add to?

numericErrors.feedback: Pairing means first WITH last: 1 + 100 = 101 — and 2 + 99, 3 + 98 all match it. The 100 alone is just one end.
50 is the NUMBER of pairs (100 terms folded in half), not what each pair adds to — that's 1 + 100 = 101.

widget.explorationFeedback: Open at least two exact sequence states before checking.

explanationVariants: One hundred terms fold into fifty equal pairs of 101.

commonErrors.feedback: 5000 is 50 · 100 — but each pair adds to 101, not 100: the 1 riding along with the 100 counts. 50 · 101 = 5050.
101 is a SINGLE pair. There are fifty of them: 50 · 101 = 5050.

steps.body: The trick generalizes to any arithmetic series. n terms fold into pairs each worth (a₁ + aₙ), and there are n/2 of them: **Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2**. Read it as an average, too: (a₁ + aₙ)/2 is the typical term, and there are n of them — which is why odd n works just as well.

commonErrors.feedback: 220 is 10 · 22 without the halving — but ten terms make only FIVE pairs of 22: 10 · 22 / 2 = 110.
200 is 10 · 20 — the last term standing in for the pair. Each pair adds FIRST and last: 2 + 20 = 22, then 10 · 22 / 2.

explanationVariants: Ten terms, pair value 55, five pairs.

commonErrors.feedback: 550 skipped the ÷ 2 — ten terms fold into just five pairs of 55: 550 / 2 = 275.
250 is 5 · 50, the two ENDS multiplied. The formula needs n times their SUM, halved: 10 · 55 / 2 = 275.

steps.body: Why exactly ÷ 2? Here's the airtight version of the fold — write the sum twice, once reversed, and add the copies column by column. Every column becomes (a₁ + aₙ), there are n columns, so **2S = n(a₁ + aₙ)**. One halving later, the formula appears. Walk it through below.

panels.title: Write it twice
panels.body: S = 3 + 5 + 7 + 9, and underneath, the same sum reversed: S = 9 + 7 + 5 + 3.

panels.title: Add the columns
panels.body: 3+9, 5+7, 7+5, 9+3 — every column is 12, the first-plus-last value. The reversal makes each column balance.

panels.title: Count the columns
panels.body: Four columns of 12: adding the two copies gives 2S = 4 · 12 = 48.

panels.title: Halve
panels.body: S = 48 / 2 = 24. And directly: 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 24. ✓ The ÷ 2 undoes the doubling from writing the sum twice.

widget.continueFeedback: Each panel is one move of the proof — keep going.
widget.successFeedback: That's the whole proof: double, balance, count, halve.

explanationVariants: Ten terms with pair value 42 fold into five pairs: 5 · 42 = 210.

commonErrors.feedback: 420 is 10 · 42 without the halving — ten terms are five pairs of 42, so 420 / 2 = 210.
189 comes from n = 9 — the count slipped. Solve 39 = 3 + (n − 1)·4: n − 1 = 9, so n = 10 terms.

hints: The formula needs n — find how many terms there are before folding.
Solve 39 = 3 + (n − 1)·4 for n, then apply S = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2.

takeaways: Ends pair to the same value — (a₁ + aₙ) every time.
Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2: n terms, half as many pairs.
The write-it-twice proof shows exactly where the ÷ 2 comes from.
steps.teaser: Next: a second form of the formula for when the last term isn't handed to you.

concept.body: The fold in miniature: 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 10. Ends pair to 11 (1+10, 2+9, …), and ten terms make five pairs: 5 · 11 = 55. The formula S = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2 says the same thing: 10 · 11 / 2.

commonErrors.feedback: 110 is 10 · 11 unhalved — ten terms fold into only FIVE pairs of 11: 55.
10 is just the last term. The whole staircase folds to 5 pairs of 11 = 55.
